meta.description: Not Dale Carnegie, not Emerson. Quote Investigator traces the line to a 1936 Los Angeles Times ad crediting Elbert Hubbard, and calls the saying anonymous.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Fear defeats more people than any other one thing in the world'?
meta.ogDescription: Carnegie quoted this line for decades and credited three different people. Quote Investigator's verdict: anonymous, earliest known print June 1936.

answer.label: Not Dale Carnegie — an anonymous saying he passed on
answer.sourceLine: Dale Carnegie did not originate this line — he quoted it as somebody else’s, and named a different author almost every time: Napoleon Bonaparte in a 1937 newspaper column, “the late Elbert Hubbard” in 1941, and Emerson in the 1962 speaking guide published under his name. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the earliest close match to a 3 June 1936 Los Angeles Times advertisement that credited Elbert Hubbard — who died in 1915 — and concludes that on current knowledge the saying is anonymous.

source.excerpt: Emerson said, “Fear defeats more people than any other one thing in the world.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ reports that the earliest close match it located appeared in a 3 June 1936 Los Angeles Times advertisement for “The Emma Dunn Method of Adult Education,” crediting Elbert Hubbard, and concludes the saying is anonymous.

The same investigation documents Carnegie’s three different credits — Napoleon Bonaparte (1937), “the late Elbert Hubbard” (1941) and Emerson (1962) — plus a 1954 book that quoted the line with no author at all (Quote Investigator ↗).

The 1962 book carrying the Emerson credit, The Quick and Easy Way to Effective Speaking, appeared after Carnegie’s death in 1955; Wikipedia ↗ describes it as compiled by his widow Dorothy Carnegie from his own notes and ideas.

Checking the Emerson end: his Society and Solitude (Boston: Fields, Osgood, & Co., 1870) does contain a chapter titled “Courage,” readable in full at Project Gutenberg ↗ — but the saying is not there. Emerson’s Wikiquote page ↗ does not list it among his sourced quotations either, and its Disputed section reaches the same verdict from the same Quote Investigator study — though it files the dispute under a garbled paraphrase of the 1870 “Courage” line, which is why searching that page for the modern wording turns up nothing.
source.excerptNote: This is the sentence that fixed the Emerson credit, and the book presents the line as Emerson’s rather than as its own. It did not fix the familiar wording: “more people…any other one thing in the world” was already in print in 1954, in Walter Lowen’s How and When to Change Your Job Successfully, with no author attached at all. The oldest printing Quote Investigator located, in 1936, reads “more men” and credits Elbert Hubbard instead. Quote Investigator found no close match for the sentence in Emerson’s writing.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted, because the wording has no identified author — Quote Investigator ↗ classes the saying as anonymous. Note that the earliest known printing (1936) and the book carrying this exact wording, The Quick and Easy Way to Effective Speaking (1962), both fall in the 1931-and-later window, so neither is a public-domain text you can quote from freely; the bare sentence simply has no traceable owner.

author.name: Dale Carnegie
author.heading: About Dale Carnegie
author.bio: Dale Carnegie was an American writer and public-speaking teacher whose 1936 bestseller How to Win Friends and Influence People made him one of the most-quoted self-improvement authors of the century. He is the reason this particular sentence is famous — he repeated it in columns and lecture material for decades — but he never claimed it, crediting Napoleon, then Elbert Hubbard, then Emerson. His habit of hanging maxims on illustrious names is exactly how an unowned line acquires a distinguished author, and how the line then drifts back onto him.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented instance: advertisement for “The Emma Dunn Method of Adult Education,” Los Angeles Times, 3 June 1936, crediting Elbert Hubbard (“Fear defeats more men than any other one thing in the world”), as documented in Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: Fear Defeats More People than Any Other One Thing in the World,” 30 October 2018 (updated 8 April 2025). The exact modern wording was already in print in Walter Lowen, How and When to Change Your Job Successfully (1954), with no author attached; the Emerson credit appears in The Quick and Easy Way to Effective Speaking (1962), published under Dale Carnegie’s name and compiled by Dorothy Carnegie after his death in 1955.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Fear defeats more people than any other one thing in the world’?” Last verified 30 Jul 2026.

copyAttribution: Not Dale Carnegie, and not Emerson. An anonymous saying: the earliest known appearance is a 3 June 1936 Los Angeles Times advertisement crediting Elbert Hubbard, who died in 1915. Carnegie credited it to Napoleon (1937) and Hubbard (1941), and the 1962 guide published under his name — compiled by Dorothy Carnegie after his death — credited Emerson. Source: Quote Investigator.

misattribution.heading: Four names, none of them documented
misattribution.intro: Few sayings have been re-assigned this often. Quote Investigator ↗ documents this sentence in print under three different famous names — Elbert Hubbard, Napoleon Bonaparte and Emerson — and found support for none of them. The fourth credit, to Dale Carnegie himself, is a modern quote-aggregator invention: no printing credits him as the author, and Quote Investigator never reviews such a claim.

items.why: Carnegie is why the line is famous, but he never claimed it: he attributed it to Napoleon in 1937, to Elbert Hubbard in 1941 and to Emerson in 1962 (Quote Investigator ↗). It is not listed among the sourced quotations on his Wikiquote page ↗ either.

The Emerson credit enters print in The Quick and Easy Way to Effective Speaking (1962) — “Emerson said…” — and was repeated by later self-help writers such as James K. Van Fleet in 1987. Quote Investigator found no close match in Emerson’s work, pointing only to a thematically related remark in his essay “Courage” (Quote Investigator ↗). It is not among the sourced quotations on Emerson’s Wikiquote page ↗ either, and that page’s Disputed section — citing the same Quote Investigator study, under a garbled paraphrase of the 1870 “Courage” line — likewise concludes the originator is unknown.

The oldest known printing of the saying already carries Hubbard’s name, in a 3 June 1936 Los Angeles Times advertisement — but Hubbard died when the Lusitania was torpedoed in 1915 ↗, and no citation from his lifetime has been found.

Carnegie wrote that Napoleon Bonaparte said fear defeats more men than any other thing in the world. No source in Napoleon’s words supports it, and Carnegie dropped the claim in later retellings (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: No author has ever been documented. In the words of Quote Investigator ↗, based on current knowledge the saying is anonymous — future researchers may uncover new citations.

context.heading: How an unowned line got three famous authors
lead: The idea was in circulation in business prose well before the phrase settled. In 1917 a writer named J. R. McCleskey argued, in an essay titled “The Prime Enemy in Business” in The Spatula, a pharmacy trade magazine, that fear was doing more to defeat success and human happiness than any other one thing — the same thought, not yet the same sentence (Quote Investigator ↗).

When the sentence does surface, it surfaces in advertising: a 3 June 1936 notice in the Los Angeles Times for a self-improvement course, with Elbert Hubbard’s name attached. From there Dale Carnegie carried it into mass circulation — and because he re-credited it each time he used it, the line accumulated authors instead of losing them. The Emerson version, printed in 1962 in the speaking guide his widow Dorothy Carnegie compiled after his death, is the one that survives on posters today.
context.detailsSummary: The attribution trail, citation by citation
detailsBody: The sequence Quote Investigator ↗ documents: 1870, the nearest real Emerson precursor, from his essay “Courage” — “He has not learned the lesson of life who does not every day surmount a fear”; May 1907, Elbert Hubbard in The Philistine — “Abolish fear and every man and woman is an orator and an artist”; December 1917, the thematic precursor in The Spatula; 3 June 1936, the Los Angeles Times advertisement crediting Elbert Hubbard, wording “more men”; March 1937, a second advertisement — in the Evening Sun of Baltimore, for the Granville B. Jacobs course — again crediting Hubbard, with no Carnegie involvement at all; November 1937, a Carnegie column crediting Napoleon Bonaparte; March 1941, a Carnegie column crediting “the late Elbert Hubbard”; 1954, Walter Lowen’s How and When to Change Your Job Successfully, which already carries the modern “more people…any other one thing in the world” wording with no author at all; 1962, The Quick and Easy Way to Effective Speaking, crediting Emerson; 1987, James K. Van Fleet’s Hidden Power, repeating the Emerson credit.

The 1954 citation is the telling one. A writer using the saying with no attribution — simply as something “truthfully said” — is a sign the line was already common property, floating free of any author, which is what makes a famous name so easy to staple onto it later.
context.pull: Printed under Carnegie’s name in 1937, 1941 and 1962 — with a different author named every time.
